paragraph.text: L26. "Vegans think they're the only ones who really defend animals"

the complaint points to a real mistake some vegans make: looking down on people who rescue and care for dogs and cats. That work saves lives and deserves respect. But the phrase generalizes, and it mixes up two things: criticizing an inconsistency (protecting some animals and paying for the death of others) and despising people. The first is legitimate and can be done respectfully; the second is a mistake. People who rescue animals already accept the main premise, that animals matter. They are a starting point, not an opponent.
L. Attacks on veganism and vegans ·
"I've been rescuing dogs for twenty years, I spend money I don't have on food and vet bills, and a vegan comes along and says I don't love animals because I eat meat. So only vegans love animals?"
Rescuers and volunteers save, treat and shelter animals, often at great personal cost.
Some vegans treat that work as worthless because the people doing it eat meat.
A movement that despises those who help animals in practice is arrogant and doesn't deserve a hearing.
So the vegan critique can be ignored.

P1 is true. P2 is true of some vegans, and it's their mistake. The problem lies in P3 and the conclusion: the bad behavior of some says nothing about the animals who are still being killed, and the question about them still stands.
fails at P3, which generalizes from a few and swaps assessing the idea for assessing the people who defend it.
"You look down on people who rescue dogs and cats."
"To you, a rescuer who eats meat is worth nothing."
"Vegans criticize rescuers but have never cleaned a kennel."
"Veganism claims a monopoly on defending animals."
"Vegans are annoying and think they are better." (which is L1)

Someone who looks after an abandoned dog is doing a very good thing, and nobody should say otherwise. Vegans want to help animals too, but they also think about pigs, cows, chickens and fish. The two groups can help each other: someone who already loves one animal can learn to care about the others as well.

People who rescue and care for animals do work that saves lives, and looking down on that is a mistake. If a vegan did that to you, they were wrong. The critique that makes sense is a different one, and it isn't against you: pigs, cows and chickens feel as dogs and cats do, and it's hard to protect some while paying for the death of others. You already believe animals matter. The conversation is only about which ones.
"What do you feel when you rescue a mistreated animal? Would a pig or a chicken deserve less?"
The phrase bundles three different claims, and each deserves its own answer:
The work of rescuers has value
Some vegans look down on that work
So the vegan critique can be ignored
No: the question about the other animals remains

Some vegans do look down on rescuers, and many vegans are rescuers, shelter volunteers and sanctuary carers. Judging all by some is the same mistake as judging all rescuers by one who mistreats animals.

text.bold: 2. Criticizing an inconsistency isn't despising a person.

paragraph.text: Saying "the animals you eat feel like the ones you rescue" is about an act, not about the worth of the person. The guide covers this difference in E13: good people also take part in unjust practices that custom accepts.

text.bold: 3. The inconsistency is real, and psychology studies it.

paragraph.text: Research on the so-called meat paradox shows that people attribute less mind and less moral importance to the animals they eat, and that simply classifying an animal as "food" is enough to make it seem to deserve less care (E11). A series of studies published in 2019 found that people give less moral value to individuals of certain species even after accounting for what they believe about those animals' intelligence and capacity to feel. The line between "pet" and "food animal" lies in custom, not in the animals.

text.bold: 4. Rescuers already accept the main premise.

paragraph.text: Someone who spends the night nursing a dog hit by a car doesn't need to be convinced that animals feel and that their lives matter. All that's left is extending this to other animals. That makes the rescuer the closest conversation partner veganism has.

text.bold: 5. The scale asks for the conversation to go on.

paragraph.text: Our World in Data records, for 2021, about 73.8 billion chickens, 1.4 billion pigs and 332 million cattle slaughtered worldwide. No rescue reaches those animals. That doesn't diminish rescue: it shows there are more animals to protect.
Eating meat reduces the moral status and mind attributed to animals
Classic study on the meat paradox
Classifying an animal as food reduces the moral standing attributed to it
The category changes the perception, not the animal
People give less moral value to individuals of certain species, even after accounting for beliefs about intelligence and sentience
Series of studies proposing a scale to measure speciesism

Part of the sense of being despised may come from expecting judgment
(d) The strongest counter-reply: those who act are worth more than those who demand consistency

The most serious version says: the rescuer gets their hands dirty, spends time and money and saves actual animals. Many vegans only changed what's on their plate and spend their time demanding consistency online. So who does more for animals?
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
Changing your plate doesn't replace helping animals who need rescue now, and vegans who only make demands should hear that.
Rescuing is helping; no longer eating animals is ceasing to cause harm. One person can do both, and many do.

text.bold: Comparing merits doesn't answer the question.

paragraph.text: Even if the rescuer does more than the vegan, the animals headed for slaughter are still there. The question was never who is the better person.

The dispute over who "really" defends animals is about people, and the animals are left out of it. For the rescued dog, what matters is having been rescued. For the pig, what matters is what happens to the pig. The moral question is about each of these individuals: if a dog's suffering moves us, what justifies ignoring that of an animal who feels in the same way?
Someone who loves animals feels accused of not loving them
L1 "Vegans are annoying and think they are better"
The feeling of being judged turns into a complaint about arrogance
E13 "He eats meat, but he's a good person"
The defense shifts to the rescuer's character
The same complaint, made by other close allies
A12 "It's natural to put our own first"
Dogs and cats would be the animals it falls to us to protect
Judges all vegans by those who look down on rescuers
The arrogance of some becomes a reason to ignore the idea
Confusing criticism of an act with contempt for the person
Any mention of the inconsistency is heard as an insult
The contest of merits takes the animals' place

text.bold: Criticizes people who don't help animals.

paragraph.text: But doesn't accept being questioned about the animals left outside their care.

text.bold: Knows that a dog feels fear and pain.

paragraph.text: And knows the reasons for thinking the same of a pig or a chicken.

text.bold: Complains about being judged by some vegans.

paragraph.text: And judges all vegans by those few.
"Pet" and "food" seem like different kinds of animal
Loving animals and eating them creates a discomfort that needs an outlet
People who feel judged disparage whoever seems to be judging
The good done for dogs and cats seems to make up for the rest
The principle being tested is: "if some defenders of a cause look down on those who help in a different way, the cause can be ignored".
Food donors criticized by people calling for changes in the law
The fight against hunger could be ignored
Hospital volunteers criticized by public health campaigners
The animals who are slaughtered could be ignored

It gets a lot right. People who rescue, treat and shelter animals do real, heavy and under-recognized work, and some vegans treat them with contempt, as if only total consistency had any value. That's unfair, and it's also bad strategy: it pushes away exactly the people who already care about animals. No one owns the defense of animals, and nobody needs to be vegan to have done an animal good.

But the value of rescue doesn't answer the question about the animals left outside it. Recognizing what the rescuer does and inviting them to look at the pig, the cow, the chicken and the fish both fit in the same conversation, as long as it's held with respect.
